extracted.intended_audience: Coast Guard leadership, MLCPAC/MLC contract specialists, Contracting Officers, COTRs, and policy makers involved with A-76 service contracting
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation of Coast Guard A-76 service contracting implementation, performance, costs, and organizational impacts, with conclusions and actionable recommendations for contracting officers, unit commanders, and policy makers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for Government employees vs civilian contractors
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether units prefer Government (military/civilian) employees or civilian contractors to perform commercial activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Majority (71%) of COs/XOs preferred Government employees; all COs/XOs with MEO winners preferred Government employees. Key reasons: more influence and flexibility in using personnel, avoidance of contract administration delays, greater trust due to access to employee background and performance history, and multi-mission capability of military personnel. Responses vary by commercial activity (e.g., security strongly preferred Government employees; food service mixed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequacy of specifications and contractor performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether Performance Work Statements (PWS), specifications, and contractor performance meet unit needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Majority considered specs and performance adequate (especially food service). Common problems: specifications perceived as too rigid and unable to anticipate changes; performance depends on who manages the contractor facility; security performance sometimes marginal; unit-level staff often lack expertise to write adequate service contract specifications; persons monitoring contracts may not be trained in Quality Assurance. Recommendation: derive better PWS/QASP, use acquisition teams, and improve COTR training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Command control over contracted activity (timeliness of responses/remedies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the command has adequate control over the contractor and whether responses and remedies to problems are timely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some commands report adequate control within contract terms. Identified problems: slow responses from MLCPAC, distance between contract site and contract administration causing slow replies, centralized contracting processes are cumbersome for changes. Recommendations include considering local contracting officer administration and streamlining contract procedures to improve timeliness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Command-contractor relationship quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Overall interpersonal and professional relationship between the command and the civilian contractor at the unit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All COs/XOs interviewed reported congenial, professional relationships regardless of their views on A-76. Examples: positive interactions with project managers and professional cooperation to meet unit needs within contract scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall perception of A-76 process and implementation
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether A-76 is viewed as a good idea and how well it was implemented in the Coast Guard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No CO/XO stated A-76 was completely good. Majority were 'qualified yes'—support the concept but cite poor Coast Guard implementation (e.g., harm to Subsistence Specialist rating, poorly planned billet reductions). Perceptions vary by activity and whether the activity is contracted-out or MEO-run. Security activities and MEO winners tended to view A-76 negatively.

rubrics_metrics.name: MEO staffing adequacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the Government's Most Efficient Organization (MEO) has sufficient personnel and appropriate grades to perform the activity effectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All respondents with MEO activities reported needing more personnel. Problems noted: MEOs are very lean; remaining personnel stretched across Pacific Area; personnel left in MEO may be too junior; non-rate enlisted shortages impacted food service MEO performance. Recommendation: reevaluate MEO staffing and consider recompetition if inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary causes of contract cost increases
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors that drive up contract costs after award.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identified primary causes: Department of Labor (DOL) wage determination increases (must be incorporated into contracts), food price increases (Producer Price Index), added work (e.g., large readiness exercises), and delays in follow-on contract awards. Continuing Resolutions (Congressional CRs) also caused many contract modifications and extra administrative work, contributing to cost increases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measures to control or mitigate contract cost increases
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical steps or contract design features that can reduce the risk or magnitude of post-award cost increases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendations include better specifications/estimates to avoid modifications for added work, estimating readiness exercise meals in original contracts, advanced planning to avoid follow-on award delays, and questioning anomalous DOL wage determinations that seem unreasonably high or low. Note: wage and food price increases are largely outside the Contracting Officer’s direct control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computation and monitoring of Government cost savings under A-76
rubrics_metrics.description: How cost savings are calculated and whether the Government continues to realize savings compared to the MEO over the contract period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Current practice computes savings as difference between initial contract award price and pre-study Government cost; this method does not account for subsequent contract cost changes. MLCPAC Contract Specialists lack access to current MEO costs after award, preventing periodic verification of ongoing savings. Recommendations: periodic comparisons of actual contract costs to current MEO, annually update cost savings computations, and adjust decisions if contract costs exceed current MEO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-award contract file maintenance and record-keeping
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards and practices for maintaining complete, consistent post-award contract documentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No standard Coast Guard post-award maintenance procedure existed, causing inconsistencies and extra work for Contract Specialists. Examples: deductions for unsatisfactory performance were not consistently recorded as cost reductions; original contract prices were sometimes hard to determine. Recommendation: implement a standardized Coast Guard-wide post-award file format and ensure deductions and modifications are accurately documented.

rubrics_metrics.name: COTR training and preparedness
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether Contracting Officer’s Technical Representatives (COTRs) receive sufficient training to perform day-to-day oversight duties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many COTRs reported training provided good basic contracting information but insufficient practical daily-duty guidance. Recommendations: review and revise COTR training to include 'lessons learned,' daily duties, designate experienced/qualified COTRs with personnel codes, and maintain them in personnel databases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contract administration responsiveness and customer orientation
rubrics_metrics.description: Contract Specialists’ proactivity in ensuring customers receive contracted services and in addressing service shortfalls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contract Specialists should increase frequency of communication and face-to-face meetings with customers, contractors, and COTRs; perform more on-site visits as necessary; actively use contract remedies for unsatisfactory performance; and incorporate needed remedies into contract modifications or future solicitations. Awareness of unique contract requirements and facility layout is important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibility determination and contractor financial condition monitoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the contracting authority adequately assesses contractor capability and financial stability to avoid performance disruptions (e.g., bankruptcy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contract Specialists should emphasize responsibility determinations and monitor contractor financial condition to avoid surprises such as Chapter 11 filings. Concern cited where contractor bankruptcy could leave insufficient in-house personnel (e.g., SS shortages) to operate facilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralization versus local contract administration
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of whether centralized contract administration creates delays or problems versus local administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Centralization (e.g., MLCPAC administering contracts distant from the unit) led to slow responses and customer dissatisfaction. Recommendation: consider local contracting officer administration for improved responsiveness in some cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of acquisition 'A-team' for developing service contracts (PWS and QASP)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a multidisciplinary team is formed to develop Performance Work Statements and Quality Assurance Surveillance Plans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendation to form service contract acquisition teams including Command CO/XO, Contract Specialist, and COTR/Unit Project Officer to ensure resources are identified and PWS/QASP meet command needs. Provide and tailor examples of past PWS/QASPs applicable to the activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incentives (or lack thereof) to save money on A-76 contracts
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether there are financial incentives for units to realize and retain savings produced by A-76 contracts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identified lack of incentive to save money: contracted units cannot use their own discretionary funds in the contract, and savings do not return to unit funds. Recommendation: consider sharing savings with units to incentivize cost control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity and availability of critical rated personnel (Subsistence Specialists)
rubrics_metrics.description: The effect of contracting-out on availability, continuity, and career path of Subsistence Specialists (SS) and similar rated personnel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problems noted: contractor implementation and billet reductions harmed SS rating; shortages of SS for operational units; no Temporary Active Duty pool of SS for augmentation; limited shore billet opportunities; contractor bankruptcy risk could leave units without qualified SS replacements. Recommendations include manpower planning and considering personnel impacts before contracting out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact of contractor project management quality on contract outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: How the quality and background of contractor project managers affect contract performance and customer satisfaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highly motivated project managers with prior military service were cited as making food service contracts work well for both contractor and customer. Quality of management and cooperation with unit leadership influence perceived contractor success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of Congressional Continuing Resolutions on contract administration workload
rubrics_metrics.description: How short-term funding measures (Continuing Resolutions) affect contract modifications, workload, and efficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuing Resolutions forced repeated partial obligation modifications, leading to a large increase in Contract Specialist workload and inefficient use of time; associated costs were not calculated. Recommendation: recognize and plan for administrative burden caused by CRs.

rubrics_metrics.name: DOL wage determination review practice
rubrics_metrics.description: How DOL wage determinations are handled and whether they are challenged when anomalous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DOL wage determination increases must be incorporated into contracts and are a primary cost driver. MLCPAC typically does not question received determinations; however, anomalously high or low determinations (e.g., Support Center Alameda security) should be questioned as they can materially affect award decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of deobligations on costs and service levels
rubrics_metrics.description: How end-of-year deobligations (when fewer meals sold than estimated) affect contract costs and service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deobligations can offset food service contract costs but are unplanned and often result in reduced service to the unit; they are not a reliable cost-control mechanism and may degrade customer satisfaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need to reevaluate or recontest MEO if inadequate
rubrics_metrics.description: When MEO workforce or scope is found inadequate, whether to review and possibly re-compete the commercial activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If more personnel are required for the Government to operate the activity, or original MEO development was incomplete or deliberately undercut, then MEOs should be reevaluated and possibly recompeted. This ensures Government retains or regains cost-effective performance capability.
